title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada checked the maps, then the wobbly cart wheel, then the breezy square. The Young Readers needed maps, but the books were still in the Library. Mayor Bell wanted the biggest parade, complete with a banner. Ada hoped usefulness could steer all that grandness in one direction.

Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said. Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.” Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

In the breezy square, the secured banner streamed above a cart loaded with maps. The Young Readers cheered and followed roads with their fingers, while Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s useful parade looked like a cheerful compass: bright, steady, and pointing toward adventure.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada hugged the library’s stack of storybooks. She wanted to deliver them to the Young Readers, who needed books, but Bram’s Shared Cart sat in the Workshop with a wobbly wheel. Mayor Bell was planning the biggest parade ever. In the still square, even a boast needed somewhere useful to go.

Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.”

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

At the square, the readers hugged their new books while Ada’s cart rested nearby. Mayor Bell welcomed them instead of bragging, and Bram’s steady wheel stayed quiet. The parade’s proudest sight was not a giant display, but a neat row of open pages and shining faces.

Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The Young Readers needed stories, and Ada had a collection ready. The trouble was a wobbly cart wheel, a breezy square, and Mayor Bell’s enormous parade plan. The books waited in the Library; the cart waited in the Workshop. Ada wondered whether this story could reach its readers.

Ada learned that the Young Readers needed stories. She hugged the storybooks. “Then these have a job,” she said. Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart. Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need stories.” His parade plan gained a wonderfully bookish purpose.

Mayor Bell puffed up to announce his biggest parade, then paused. “A helpful parade sounds better,” he decided. He chose the readers’ need over his boast.

Ada delivered the story collection to the Young Readers. “Fresh stories, straight to the square,” she said, and the books were ready for their waiting audience.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The secured banner fluttered above the storybooks as breezy Parade Square rang with cheers. The Young Readers opened pages, Mayor Bell welcomed them, and Ada watched the cart hold steady. It looked like a story’s happy ending made visible: bright cloth overhead, eager readers below, and adventure beginning everywhere.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The Young Readers needed books, and Ada had them. Unfortunately, the Shared Cart’s wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop, while a breeze whisked across Parade Square. Mayor Bell was busy promising the biggest parade. Ada hoped his promise could survive both a wobble and the wind.

Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.”

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The breezy square filled with cheers as the secured banner lifted and settled above the book cart. Young Readers held their books close, Ada smiled, and Mayor Bell welcomed the crowd. The banner fluttered like a bright flag on a helpful ship, while every reader stayed happily on course.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada wanted to deliver useful maps from the Library. The Young Readers needed maps, but the books waited on a cart whose wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop. Mayor Bell promised the biggest parade in town. Ada wondered whether his grand plan could find its way to the children.

Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.”

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The parade ended with maps spread across the square like little blue-and-green windows. The Young Readers traced roads with eager fingers, while Mayor Bell welcomed them and Ada watched her cart do useful work. Even the grandest parade had finally found a sensible destination.

Ada wanted to deliver useful maps from the Library. The Young Readers needed maps, but the books waited on a cart whose wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop. Mayor Bell promised the biggest parade in town. Ada wondered whether his grand plan could find its way to the children.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The parade ended with maps spread across the square like little blue-and-green windows. The Young Readers traced roads with eager fingers, while Mayor Bell welcomed them and Ada watched her cart do useful work. Even the grandest parade had finally found a sensible destination.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The books were ready, and the cart wheel was ready too. The missing pieces were togetherness and calm: the books waited in the Library, the cart in the Workshop, and wind brushed Parade Square. Mayor Bell wanted the biggest parade. Ada wanted it to carry something truly useful.

Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The breezy square filled with cheers as the secured banner lifted and settled above the book cart. Young Readers held their books close, Ada smiled, and Mayor Bell welcomed the crowd. The banner fluttered like a bright flag on a helpful ship, while every reader stayed happily on course.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The stories were ready in the Library, and the cart was ready in the Workshop. Outside, a breeze waited in Parade Square, and Mayor Bell planned a parade of enormous size. The Young Readers needed stories. Ada wanted the enormous plan to deliver something delightfully readable.

Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed stories. She hugged the storybooks. “Then these have a job,” she said. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need stories.” His parade plan gained a wonderfully bookish purpose. Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Mayor Bell puffed up to announce his biggest parade, then paused. “A helpful parade sounds better,” he decided. He chose the readers’ need over his boast.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada delivered the story collection to the Young Readers. “Fresh stories, straight to the square,” she said, and the books were ready for their waiting audience.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The secured banner fluttered above the storybooks as breezy Parade Square rang with cheers. The Young Readers opened pages, Mayor Bell welcomed them, and Ada watched the cart hold steady. It looked like a story’s happy ending made visible: bright cloth overhead, eager readers below, and adventure beginning everywhere.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada wanted to deliver useful maps from the Library. The Young Readers needed maps, but the books waited on a cart whose wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop. Mayor Bell promised the biggest parade in town. Ada wondered whether his grand plan could find its way to the children.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

Around Ada’s cart, the Young Readers studied maps and pointed to winding rivers and faraway towns. Mayor Bell’s welcoming parade gathered them close, while the pages supplied the biggest view of all: a whole world tucked neatly into their hands.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The stories were ready in the Library, and the cart was ready in the Workshop. Outside, a breeze waited in Parade Square, and Mayor Bell planned a parade of enormous size. The Young Readers needed stories. Ada wanted the enormous plan to deliver something delightfully readable.

Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed stories. She hugged the storybooks. “Then these have a job,” she said. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need stories.” His parade plan gained a wonderfully bookish purpose. Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said.

Mayor Bell puffed up to announce his biggest parade, then paused. “A helpful parade sounds better,” he decided. He chose the readers’ need over his boast.

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada delivered the story collection to the Young Readers. “Fresh stories, straight to the square,” she said, and the books were ready for their waiting audience.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The secured banner fluttered above the storybooks as breezy Parade Square rang with cheers. The Young Readers opened pages, Mayor Bell welcomed them, and Ada watched the cart hold steady. It looked like a story’s happy ending made visible: bright cloth overhead, eager readers below, and adventure beginning everywhere.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The books were ready, and the cart wheel was ready too. The missing pieces were togetherness and calm: the books waited in the Library, the cart in the Workshop, and wind brushed Parade Square. Mayor Bell wanted the biggest parade. Ada wanted it to carry something truly useful.

Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The banner tugged at its fastenings, but held firm above the delivered books. Beneath it, delighted Young Readers cheered as Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s cart stood steady in the breeze, turning the square into a bright, book-filled harbor.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada wanted to deliver useful books to the Young Readers, who needed books. The Library Books were ready, and Bram’s cart had a ready wheel, but the cart still waited in the Workshop. Mayor Bell planned the biggest parade. Ada needed that grand plan to point toward the readers.

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

At the square, the readers hugged their new books while Ada’s cart rested nearby. Mayor Bell welcomed them instead of bragging, and Bram’s steady wheel stayed quiet. The parade’s proudest sight was not a giant display, but a neat row of open pages and shining faces.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada wanted to deliver useful maps from the Library. The Young Readers needed maps, but the books waited on a cart whose wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop. Mayor Bell promised the biggest parade in town. Ada wondered whether his grand plan could find its way to the children.

Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

Around Ada’s cart, the Young Readers studied maps and pointed to winding rivers and faraway towns. Mayor Bell’s welcoming parade gathered them close, while the pages supplied the biggest view of all: a whole world tucked neatly into their hands.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The map books stood ready in the Library, and the Shared Cart’s wheel was ready in the Workshop. Yet the readers still needed maps, the square was breezy, and Mayor Bell wanted a gigantic parade. Ada pictured a banner, a cart, and one very useful destination.

Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.” Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration. Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

In the breezy square, the secured banner streamed above a cart loaded with maps. The Young Readers cheered and followed roads with their fingers, while Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s useful parade looked like a cheerful compass: bright, steady, and pointing toward adventure.

story:
The stories were ready in the Library, and the cart was ready in the Workshop. Outside, a breeze waited in Parade Square, and Mayor Bell planned a parade of enormous size. The Young Readers needed stories. Ada wanted the enormous plan to deliver something delightfully readable.

With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the story collection to the Young Readers. “Fresh stories, straight to the square,” she said, and the books were ready for their waiting audience.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The secured banner fluttered above the storybooks as breezy Parade Square rang with cheers. The Young Readers opened pages, Mayor Bell welcomed them, and Ada watched the cart hold steady. It looked like a story’s happy ending made visible: bright cloth overhead, eager readers below, and adventure beginning everywhere.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The books were ready, and the cart wheel was ready too. The missing pieces were togetherness and calm: the books waited in the Library, the cart in the Workshop, and wind brushed Parade Square. Mayor Bell wanted the biggest parade. Ada wanted it to carry something truly useful.

Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger. Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The banner tugged at its fastenings, but held firm above the delivered books. Beneath it, delighted Young Readers cheered as Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s cart stood steady in the breeze, turning the square into a bright, book-filled harbor.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada wanted to deliver useful storybooks to the Young Readers, who needed stories. The books waited in the Library, but the Shared Cart’s wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop. Mayor Bell planned the biggest parade. Ada hoped the parade could bring more than noise.

Ada learned that the Young Readers needed stories. She hugged the storybooks. “Then these have a job,” she said.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need stories.” His parade plan gained a wonderfully bookish purpose. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble.

Mayor Bell puffed up to announce his biggest parade, then paused. “A helpful parade sounds better,” he decided. He chose the readers’ need over his boast.

With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the story collection to the Young Readers. “Fresh stories, straight to the square,” she said, and the books were ready for their waiting audience.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The Young Readers gathered around the delivered story collection, delighted faces glowing above the pages. Mayor Bell welcomed them, and Ada’s cart stood proudly nearby. In the square, the parade looked less like a noisy show and more like a storybook come alive—one reader, one page, one happy gasp at a time.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The Young Readers needed books, and Ada had them. Unfortunately, the Shared Cart’s wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop, while a breeze whisked across Parade Square. Mayor Bell was busy promising the biggest parade. Ada hoped his promise could survive both a wobble and the wind.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said. Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The banner tugged at its fastenings, but held firm above the delivered books. Beneath it, delighted Young Readers cheered as Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s cart stood steady in the breeze, turning the square into a bright, book-filled harbor.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada hugged the library’s stack of storybooks. She wanted to deliver them to the Young Readers, who needed books, but Bram’s Shared Cart sat in the Workshop with a wobbly wheel. Mayor Bell was planning the biggest parade ever. In the still square, even a boast needed somewhere useful to go.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

The Shared Cart stood in the still square, piled with useful books and ringed by delighted Young Readers. Mayor Bell’s welcoming wave was smaller than his old boast, but Ada’s grin was enormous. The parade had become a bright little library on wheels, with pages opening like windows.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The books were ready, and the cart wheel was ready too. The missing pieces were togetherness and calm: the books waited in the Library, the cart in the Workshop, and wind brushed Parade Square. Mayor Bell wanted the biggest parade. Ada wanted it to carry something truly useful.

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The banner tugged at its fastenings, but held firm above the delivered books. Beneath it, delighted Young Readers cheered as Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s cart stood steady in the breeze, turning the square into a bright, book-filled harbor.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada wanted to deliver useful maps from the Library. The Young Readers needed maps, but the books waited on a cart whose wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop. Mayor Bell promised the biggest parade in town. Ada wondered whether his grand plan could find its way to the children.

Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.”

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

Around Ada’s cart, the Young Readers studied maps and pointed to winding rivers and faraway towns. Mayor Bell’s welcoming parade gathered them close, while the pages supplied the biggest view of all: a whole world tucked neatly into their hands.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The stories were ready in the Library, and the cart was ready in the Workshop. Outside, a breeze waited in Parade Square, and Mayor Bell planned a parade of enormous size. The Young Readers needed stories. Ada wanted the enormous plan to deliver something delightfully readable.

Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed stories. She hugged the storybooks. “Then these have a job,” she said. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need stories.” His parade plan gained a wonderfully bookish purpose.

Mayor Bell puffed up to announce his biggest parade, then paused. “A helpful parade sounds better,” he decided. He chose the readers’ need over his boast.

Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance.

Ada delivered the story collection to the Young Readers. “Fresh stories, straight to the square,” she said, and the books were ready for their waiting audience.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The secured banner fluttered above the storybooks as breezy Parade Square rang with cheers. The Young Readers opened pages, Mayor Bell welcomed them, and Ada watched the cart hold steady. It looked like a story’s happy ending made visible: bright cloth overhead, eager readers below, and adventure beginning everywhere.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The books were ready, and the cart wheel was ready too. The missing pieces were togetherness and calm: the books waited in the Library, the cart in the Workshop, and wind brushed Parade Square. Mayor Bell wanted the biggest parade. Ada wanted it to carry something truly useful.

Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said. Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. The banner tugged at its fastenings, but held firm above the delivered books. Beneath it, delighted Young Readers cheered as Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s cart stood steady in the breeze, turning the square into a bright, book-filled harbor.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The books were ready, and the cart wheel was ready too. The missing pieces were togetherness and calm: the books waited in the Library, the cart in the Workshop, and wind brushed Parade Square. Mayor Bell wanted the biggest parade. Ada wanted it to carry something truly useful.

Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The banner tugged at its fastenings, but held firm above the delivered books. Beneath it, delighted Young Readers cheered as Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s cart stood steady in the breeze, turning the square into a bright, book-filled harbor.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada wanted to deliver useful maps from the Library. The Young Readers needed maps, but the books waited on a cart whose wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop. Mayor Bell promised the biggest parade in town. Ada wondered whether his grand plan could find its way to the children.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.” Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

Around Ada’s cart, the Young Readers studied maps and pointed to winding rivers and faraway towns. Mayor Bell’s welcoming parade gathered them close, while the pages supplied the biggest view of all: a whole world tucked neatly into their hands.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The Young Readers needed books, and Ada had them. Unfortunately, the Shared Cart’s wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop, while a breeze whisked across Parade Square. Mayor Bell was busy promising the biggest parade. Ada hoped his promise could survive both a wobble and the wind.

Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The breezy square filled with cheers as the secured banner lifted and settled above the book cart. Young Readers held their books close, Ada smiled, and Mayor Bell welcomed the crowd. The banner fluttered like a bright flag on a helpful ship, while every reader stayed happily on course.

She hugged the storybooks. “Then these have a job,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need stories.” His parade plan gained a wonderfully bookish purpose. title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada hugged the library’s stack of storybooks. She wanted to deliver them to the Young Readers, who needed books, but Bram’s Shared Cart sat in the Workshop with a wobbly wheel. Mayor Bell was planning the biggest parade ever. In the still square, even a boast needed somewhere useful to go.

Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the books delivered and the square still, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade. He waved toward Ada’s cart and invited everyone to celebrate reading, not merely his own grandness.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

At the square, the readers hugged their new books while Ada’s cart rested nearby. Mayor Bell welcomed them instead of bragging, and Bram’s steady wheel stayed quiet. The parade’s proudest sight was not a giant display, but a neat row of open pages and shining faces.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
Ada checked the maps, then the wobbly cart wheel, then the breezy square. The Young Readers needed maps, but the books were still in the Library. Mayor Bell wanted the biggest parade, complete with a banner. Ada hoped usefulness could steer all that grandness in one direction.

Ada discovered that the Young Readers needed maps. She held up the map books. “At last,” she said, “a parade can point somewhere.”

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need maps.” His parade could now carry directions instead of only decoration. Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said. Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble.

Mayor Bell began, “My biggest parade will—” Then he considered the waiting readers. “Actually, it will help them.” He chose usefulness and set boasting aside.

With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the maps to the Young Readers. “Here are adventures with directions,” she said, placing the useful books where the readers could use them.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

In the breezy square, the secured banner streamed above a cart loaded with maps. The Young Readers cheered and followed roads with their fingers, while Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s useful parade looked like a cheerful compass: bright, steady, and pointing toward adventure.

title: The Parade That Helped
story:
The Young Readers needed books, and Ada had them. Unfortunately, the Shared Cart’s wheel wobbled in Bram’s Workshop, while a breeze whisked across Parade Square. Mayor Bell was busy promising the biggest parade. Ada hoped his promise could survive both a wobble and the wind.

In the Workshop, Bram knelt beside the Shared Cart. He tightened and tested the wobbly wheel until it held firm. “There,” he said. “Now it can roll instead of wobble like pudding.”

Mayor Bell carried his Parade Banner from Town Hall to Parade Square. He held it upright, though the breeze immediately tried to give it a dance. Ada learned that the Young Readers needed books. She tapped the book stack. “Good thing I have exactly the useful sort.” Ada noticed that Parade Square was breezy. She watched the air tug at an imaginary ribbon. “The banner will need a firm grip,” she said. Bram handed Ada the cart handle. “It’s yours to use,” he said. Ada gripped it carefully; the cart was now hers to roll, though Bram remained its lending owner. Ada told Mayor Bell, “The Young Readers need books.” His enormous parade plan suddenly had a very practical passenger.

Mayor Bell lifted his chin for a boast, then lowered it. “A biggest parade is fine,” he said, “but a helpful parade is better.” He chose a plan for books and stopped boasting.

Ada told Mayor Bell, “The square is breezy.” He glanced at the banner. “Then it needs less waving and more holding,” he said.

Mayor Bell secured the banner against the breeze. “There,” he said. “It may flutter, but it will not fly off to start its own parade.”

Ada rolled the Shared Cart from the Workshop to Parade Square. Its ready wheel turned smoothly, without even one pudding wobble. With the cart waiting in Parade Square, Ada brought the Library Books there. She kept both hands on the stack and set it safely on the cart.

Ada delivered the storybooks to the Young Readers. “A parade with pages!” she announced. The books were now ready for the readers who needed them.

With the banner secured and the books delivered, Mayor Bell led a welcoming book parade through the breezy square. The banner shone above the cart without escaping.

The Young Readers cheered when the parade arrived with books. Their waiting faces brightened, and their delighted applause made the cart handles tremble.

The banner tugged at its fastenings, but held firm above the delivered books. Beneath it, delighted Young Readers cheered as Mayor Bell welcomed them. Ada’s cart stood steady in the breeze, turning the square into a bright, book-filled harbor.
